summary:
Mission Control is an interactive web game where students design, launch and operate a space mission over 12 months. The player builds a satellite from a bus, power source, instruments, thermal control, pointing and communications, then assembles the rocket part by part, from the bottom up. Before launch, an eight-item checklist reviews mass, power, data, temperature, reliability and budget, and each item leads to the step where it can be fixed. The player then makes decisions during events such as solar storms or antenna failures, and performance is scored out of 1,000 points. Parts and missions are based on real catalogs from NASA, ESA and NOAA. The game is available in Spanish and English and adapts to desktop, tablet and phone.

The challenge asks students to experience a complete mission, from concept to operations, where every engineering decision has consequences. Students rarely see that full cycle, and trade-offs between mass, power, cost and orbit tend to stay abstract. Our approach makes them concrete: changing one instrument affects power, data, budget and the chance of success all at once, and the final report explains what caused the grade.

It matters because it brings space engineering within reach of people who have no access to it. Beyond teaching, the game forces players to manage limited resources, which is useful in any engineering project.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Mission Control is a web simulator where the player designs and operates a complete space mission. The player chooses one of six missions in two categories, Eye on Earth and Space Telescope, each with its budget, deadline and orbit. First, they design the satellite in the workshop: bus, power, instruments, thermal control, pointing, communications and propulsion. Then they build the rocket part by part, from the bottom up: Stage 1, boosters, upper stage and fairing. Stage 1 decides which parts are compatible, and each choice changes mass, power, data, cost and reliability. Before launch, an eight-item review marks each area green, yellow or red, and tapping an item takes the player to the step where it can be fixed. If the design is valid, the launch has a chance of success that depends on the reliability of the rocket and the satellite. Then, over 12 months, the spacecraft faces events such as solar storms, antenna failures or degrading instruments, and the player decides how to respond each time. At the end, they receive a grade out of 1,000 points, with a report that explains what caused each result.

What benefits does it have?

It teaches the full cycle of a mission, from concept to operations, and makes the trade-offs between mass, power, cost and orbit visible. Students immediately see how changing one instrument affects several areas at once. It also teaches how to manage limited resources and make decisions under risk. It is free, runs in the browser with nothing to install, and adapts to computer, tablet and phone.

What is the expected impact?

We want students who rarely encounter space engineering to understand it in a hands-on way, and we want teachers to have a tool for discussing systems design without specialized equipment. The game also shows real parts and missions from NASA, ESA and NOAA, which brings those references to a wide audience. Impact will be measured through actual use of the game, for example how many games are completed and what grades players earn.

What tools, languages or software did we use?

We built everything with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks or external runtime dependencies. The satellite and rocket graphics are SVG generated by code, and the game state is saved in the browser with localStorage. We used Node.js for automated tests of the game logic and Playwright to test the screens on desktop, tablet and phone. The site is published on Vercel, the code is on GitHub, and we manage version control with Git. For the design we used the Nunito font and a dark palette. We did not use any special hardware.

How is the project creative?

It combines a technical simulator with game mechanics. The rocket is assembled part by part, like in modular building games, and the review checklist works like a control panel. The operations events force decisions with incomplete information, and the hint button guides the player without revealing the correct answer. The missions are based on real projects, so players learn NASA history and references while they play. The game can also be played in two languages.

What factors did the team consider?

We took into account that the audience does not always have experience in space engineering, so every term has an entry in the glossary and every screen explains what to do. We considered technical accuracy: mass, power and capacity values come from real catalogs, and the values not found in the catalog are documented for review. We made sure the game works on any device, requires no installation, and saves progress without an account. We also thought about language accessibility, so it can be played in Spanish or English, and about fairness: the Rookie difficulty lets people learn without pressure, while Expert demands precision.
